thesis: The market's automation race is a Prisoner's Dilemma that competitive pressures will inevitably lose, regardless of what individual firms choose to do.
hook: Block just fired 5,000 people because AI made them 'unnecessary' — and economists have now proven mathematically why every other company will do the same, even when it destroys the economy for everyone.
stakes: When every firm automate to maximize their own profits, they collectively crater consumer demand. The deadweight loss formula is N times L times (demand loss minus cost saving) — and the wedge grows with competition. This isn't a tech sector blip; it's a structural trap baked into how markets work.
counterpoint: A monopolist would internalize this externality perfectly — which is cold comfort to anyone who prefers competition to monopoly, and raises the uncomfortable question of whether the cure is worse than the disease.
implication: No amount of executive hand-wringing, industry pledges, or government jawboning can fix a game where defection is strictly dominant. Either we build coordination mechanisms that don't rely on trust, or we accept the steady hollowing out of middle-class consumer demand.
close: Dorsey predicted most companies would reach the same conclusion within a year. He wasn't being cynical — he was being game-theoretically honest. The question isn't whether your job will be automated. It's whether automation will happen before or after the demand to buy anything collapses.
warnings: most evidence is secondary reporting on a primary academic source
prediction claim (Dorsey's timeline) is medium confidence
